title: Disaster in Indiana Leaves Thousands Without Power
seoTitle: Indiana Storm Leaves Thousands Without Power for Weeks
subtitle: A wave of 99 mph winds caused blackouts that lasted for more than two weeks
excerpt: A 99 mph storm hit northwest Indiana on August 11, knocking down trees and power lines.
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
On August 11, a storm with 99 mph winds struck northwest Indiana, knocking down trees and power lines and leaving thousands of residents without electricity for more than 12 days.

Outages in Gary and Surrounding Areas

In the city of Gary, about 9,000 customers remained without power until August 23. Mayor Eddie Melton stated in a video that "twelve days is too long" for families, businesses, and children. The Northern Indiana Public Service Company (NIPSCO) reported that, as of August 23, nearly 16,500 accounts were still without power. The company planned to restore power in Munster by midnight on August 24 and in Gary and Portage by August 25, but warned that the timeline may vary due to local damage.

National Guard Intervention and State Investigation

Governor Mike Braun declared a state of emergency on August 13 and mobilized the National Guard to assist NIPSCO crews. On August 20, he asked the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission (IURC) to investigate NIPSCO, alleging that the company failed to maintain infrastructure and restore service quickly. The investigation will also cover the use of state funds for improvements.

Impact on the Gary Community

Melissa Dixon, a Gary resident, reported on August 22 that after 12 days without power, she was trying to feed her family with free food and generators. She described the discomfort of having to walk to distribution points and dealing with food spoilage and a lack of refrigeration. NIPSCO predicts that power in Gary will not be fully restored until the end of Tuesday.

Storm Characteristics

The National Weather Service preliminarily classified the storm as a "derecho," a widespread straight-line wind storm phenomenon with winds of at least 58 mph and a damage path of 250 miles. The final analysis will be completed in 2027. The storm also produced several tornadoes, two of which crossed the border into Illinois.

Responses from Authorities and the Power Company

NIPSCO stated that it has hired additional crews and sought support from neighboring utilities to accelerate restoration. The August 23 statement emphasized that "no outage will be overlooked." Meanwhile, the mayor and governor continue to push for speed and accountability from the company.

With information from USA Today, WSBT, Chicago Sun-Times.
